title: IMF's 20% US Crash Scenario Is a Diversification Test for NRI Portfolios
excerpt: The Fund's downside case — a roughly 20% fall in US stocks if AI productivity disappoints — lands hardest on households whose 401(k), RSUs and brokerage all ride the same mega-cap trade.
body:
• The IMF's October outlook models a downside scenario in which US stocks fall about 20% if the AI investment boom fails to deliver expected productivity gains.
  • For an NRI household with $250,000 in US equities, a 20% fall is a $50,000 paper loss — concentration, not timing, is the controllable risk.
  • Advisers cited by Mint suggest capping global/US exposure at a deliberate share of the portfolio (one suggests around 20%) rather than letting a single market dominate by default.
  • The IMF simultaneously raised India's growth forecast to 7% for FY27 and FY28 and global growth to 3.1% for 2026 — the warning is about valuations, not an imminent-crash call.

The International Monetary Fund has put a number on the risk that US-heavy portfolios now carry. In its October outlook, the Fund warns that if the AI investment boom fails to produce the productivity gains investors have priced in, US stocks could fall by around 20% in a downside scenario, with global growth weakening thereafter, as Mint's summary of the outlook reports. The same report raised India's growth forecast to 7% for both FY27 and FY28 and lifted the 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% — a reminder that this is a valuation warning inside an otherwise firm outlook, not a forecast of collapse.

Why NRIs Are Exposed Differently

Indian professionals in the United States typically hold US equities three times over without planning to: a 401(k) defaulted into US large-cap funds, RSUs concentrated in their own employer's stock, and a brokerage account tilted to the same mega-cap technology names driving the AI trade. A 20% index fall does not hit those three pots independently — it hits them together, in the same weeks that technology-sector job risk rises. That correlation, not the headline number, is the actual exposure.

What Diversification Actually Buys

The arithmetic cuts both ways, which is the point. Mint's expert roadmap, in a Mint analysis of global allocation, works through a two-year example from Wise Finserv's Ajay Kumar Yadav: a ₹1 crore India-only portfolio split between the Nifty 50 and Nifty 500 would have ended near ₹92 lakh, while a 70:30 India-global portfolio — 15% each in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 — reached roughly ₹1.08 crore, helped by dollar gains and rupee weakness, before expenses and taxes. The same analysis notes the mirror image: in 2022 the Nasdaq-100 fell about 33% while the Nifty 50 total return index gained roughly 5.7%, and the India-heavy investor looked smarter.

Emkay Wealth Management's Joseph Thomas, quoted in the same piece, puts a discipline on it: global exposure limited to about 20% of the portfolio, treated as a complement to domestic holdings rather than a substitute. For US-based NRIs the direction reverses — the "global" diversifier is India and other non-US markets — but the principle is identical: a fixed, reviewed allocation instead of whatever a single employer's equity plan happens to produce.

The Practical Checklist

Three moves follow from the IMF scenario without requiring a market call. First, measure concentration honestly: add the 401(k), RSUs and brokerage together and calculate the true US mega-cap share. Second, set a target band for non-US exposure — for many dual-country households that includes Indian equity held through the routes open to NRIs — and rebalance into it on a schedule rather than in a panic. Third, keep the emergency fund and any money earmarked for near-term goals such as a home deposit outside equities entirely, so a 20% drawdown never forces a sale.

The IMF is not predicting the fall; it is stress-testing what happens if AI spending disappoints. Portfolios built to survive the stress test do not need to forecast it.
